rows.what: A new page: «Lives on one scale» — every dated person in a line, as a scrollable chart of lifespans
rows.src: Built from roster.json; no new research
rows.text:
**David asked whether the births and deaths of a whole line could be shown on a scrollable timeline.** *[The Timeline](/timeline/) already existed and is deliberately a different thing — its own dek says* «the point is not when people were born» — *so this is the one that is about the people.* **[/lives/](/lives/)**: *one bar to a person, birth to death, sorted by birth, scrolling sideways across the years and down through the line.*

**⭐ The point of it is not the bars. It is which bars are solid.** *A bar is drawn* **solid** *only where the roster says the date was* **read off a register, an index of record or a headstone**; *everything else came off a family tree and is drawn* **hollow**. *Across the roster that is **431 hollow of 1,031**;* ***on our own Carnia line it is 100 of 205 — almost exactly half.*** **The hollow bars are the work still to do, and the chart is the first thing on this site that shows how much of it there is.**

**And an open end is not a short life.** *Where only one date is known the bar fades out instead of stopping square.* ***57 per cent of these people have one date and not the other*** — *which is, mostly, a map of the burial registers nobody has read.*

**What it leaves out, and why.** *All* **58 living people**, *entirely — the rule here is name and town and nothing else, and a chart of dates is no place for an exception.* *And* **28 rows the roster marks** `sameAs` *another: they are one life entered twice, and one life gets one bar.*

**It is generated from `roster.json` and nothing is typed into it** — *including the figures in its own prose, which compute themselves so that a sentence like* «almost exactly half» *cannot go stale the next time somebody reads a register.*

**⚠ It is not in the navigation.** *The nav is shared ground with another session; the page is reachable from [the Timeline](/timeline/) until David decides where it belongs.*

rows.what: Fourteen places where the tree and this archive disagree now say so on the person's own page
rows.text:
Seven are **age arithmetic** — death agreed, birth out by one to three — and now say plainly that *an age produces this* and that the archive keeps the register's figure. Two are **too big for arithmetic** (*Mario*, 1919 against 1924; *Girolamo of Omiš*, 1632 against 1622) and say **one side has the wrong man**. Three dispute the **death year** — *Clementina Maria* by thirty years, *Josephus Lambertus* by twenty-one, *Lina* by two — and say **this needs the burial register, not a judgement**. And the mirrored *Petrus Defranceschi* pair says it is **one man on the roster twice**, 1768 and 1765, same death year 1829.

**A first attempt put these notes on 56 rows instead of 14**, because it matched on name alone and this roster is record-level: *Maria Defranceschi* is twenty-four rows, and twenty-three of them would have been accused of a disagreement belonging to one. Stripped and redone against **name and source**.

rows.what: Eighty-four people were in the roster with no link to their own page — and the pages existed all along
rows.src: The roster audited against its own dossiers
rows.text:
**Nothing was missing. Eighty-four rows just had nowhere to click.**

The sweep for connections turned up 84 roster rows whose `who` field was empty — **63 of them from the index**, the rest from households, register reads and line notes. The reading at the time was that these people had no page, and so **nothing in the archive could link to them**: they were unreachable by construction, the cheapest kind of disconnection there is.

**That reading was wrong in the best possible way.** `build-dossiers.py` writes a page for **every** roster row, keyed on `slugify(name)` — it never consults the `who` field at all. So all eighty-four pages had been built, and published, and were sitting at their URLs. What was missing was the **link from the roster to them**.

**Checked before touching anything:** all 84 slugs were already present in `dossiers.json`. **Backfilled: 84. Skipped: 0. Roster rows now without a page link: none.**

**Four rows were deliberately left alone** — the Lerena family, whose `who` points at `/cheryl-lerena/` rather than a `/who/` page, because that research belongs to another session.

*A reminder that «this person is unreachable» and «this person has no page» are different claims, and only one of them was true.*

rows.what: The «forty-five duplicate rows» were the roster working as designed — but the long baptismal names really were split, and now join up
rows.src: The merge list, tested against the roster's own contract
rows.text:
**The merge was the wrong fix, and checking the page's own note said so.**

The audit of 20 September found 38 groups and 45 roster rows that looked like one person entered twice or seven times. **The roster's own note answers it:** *«Identity here is by record, not by resolved individual — two entries may be one person»*. A row is a **record**, not a human. Pietro De Franceschi b. 1734 appears seven times because seven records name him, and collapsing them would delete the provenance the page exists to show. **Nothing was merged.**

**And the dossiers already resolve what matters.** `build-dossiers.py` groups rows by slug, so one page carries *«Found in: Household · Parish burial · Read off the register · Record index»*, and a second pass cross-links the spellings, so **Mattio De Franceschi** already reached its eight variants.

**One real hole underneath it, though.** That fold keeps the **whole** name, so it never joined a long baptismal name to its own short form. Fiume christened a boy **«Franciscum Josephum Aloysium Joannem Nepomuc»** in 1797 and the index carried him at **four different lengths** — four pages, one child, not a link between them. **Camillo Romano never reached Camillo** either.

**Fixed by a second pass on first given name plus birth year** — specific enough to mean something, and exactly the case the first pass misses. It only ever adds. **77 groups, 147 pages, 101 cross-links that were missing.** Camillo now reaches Camillo Romano; the four Franciscums reach each other and Franciscus.

*Three times today a finding dissolved when the archive's own files were checked. This is the third, and the residue was worth more than the claim.*

rows.what: Twenty-one people who looked like they were in two places at once, worked through one at a time
rows.src: The cross-place candidates from the roster audit
rows.text:
**Seven were never in two places. Six are probably two different people. Six need a register. And two rows of this archive were carrying a page slug where a place should be.**

**Not two places at all — seven.** **Anton Rudolf b. 1890** is «Klenovica» and «Ledenice», and **Klenovica is in Ledenice parish** — the thing this archive read on the page this morning. **Antonio b. 1897** is «Middle Village» and «Queens», and Middle Village *is* Queens. **Camillo b. 1868** is «Gologorica» and «Pazin» because the second row is the deliberate namesake entry for his name in Croatian. **Giuseppe b. 1784** and **Katharina Johanna b. 1823** are paired against «Croatia, parish not named» and «Austria» — **placeholders, not places**. **Giovanni Eliseo b. 1825** is Pula and Fažana, eight kilometres apart, and the index geocodes Fažana to **Fasana in Piedmont**, which is how it became a country apart.

**A real defect underneath, now fixed.** Four `life` rows had a **page section slug in the `place` field** — `early-fiume`, `carnia-fiume`, `pazin-fiume` — so their dossiers read *«Place: early-fiume»*. They are **Valentino Defranceschi**, **Domenico de Franceschi**, **Giovanni Battista Defranceschi** and **Zuane De Franceschi**, and they do **not** all resolve the same way: the first three belong at **Rijeka**, but Zuane is **of Mione in Carnia** and only appears in the Fiume page's Carnian section. Set accordingly, with their place slugs.

**Probably two different people — six.** **Antonio b. 1753** is at Rijeka, Split and Vodnjan; **Stefano b. 1831** is at Vodnjan three times and at **Omiš** once, on the chart, which is a different line entirely. And **four pit the Gologorica pedigree against a burial somewhere else** — **Antonius b. 1848** (Pula), **Franciscus b. 1819** and **Josephus b. 1862** (both Kaštelir), **Joannes b. 1871** (Ližnjan). *Four of the same shape is worth noticing, but a common forename and a shared year in a small surname pool is exactly what coincidence looks like, and this archive is not merging a pedigree into a burial on that.*

**Still open — six.** Anna Maria b. 1844 (Poreč / Fiume), Franco b. 1821 (Rijeka / Vižinada), Mattio b. 1674 (Svetvinčenat / Rovinj), Piero Anto b. 1736 (Rovinj / Pula), Pietro b. 1734 (Svetvinčenat / Bale / Vodnjan) and Pietro b. 1884 (Rijeka / **Giubiasco in Ticino**). **Each is one register entry away and none of them is guessed at here.**

rows.what: Two cut strips laid on a blank leaf
rows.text:
Frame 567 is **the same opening as 566, photographed a second time** with **two cut strips of a register page** laid on the facing leaf. The strips are not new material: their house numbers — **592, 600, 159, 75, 78, 102** — are page 164's entries 11 to 17, which frame 566 already shows in place.

**This changes how the film has to be counted.** Consecutive frames share a page, and some frames are re-shoots of a page already filmed. **581 frames is not 581 pages**, and any estimate of how long this book takes to read that is built on the frame count is wrong. The reliable unit is the **book's own page number**, written at the top outer corner, with the **entry numbers** as the check that nothing has been skipped between them.
